newsitem.title: USA: Plan fizzles to convert Spartanburg, S.C., loan.
newsitem.headline: Plan fizzles to convert Spartanburg, S.C., loan.

text.p: South Carolina's Spartanburg Sanitary Sewer System failed to attract any bidders Monday with an unusual attempt to convert a low-cost state loan to private placement GO debt, bond counsel Steve Matthews said.
"They knew it was a long shot," Matthews said after the noon deadline passed without any bidders.

The special purpose district is six years into a 20-year loan from a state agency, the South Carolina Water Quality Revolving Fund Authority, which administers the state water pollution control revolving fund.

The state loan had an interest rate of 4.75 percent and required the system to make quarterly payments of $176,398.92. The system wanted to convert the revenue debt to general obligation debt, and will proceed with that part of the plan by amending the loan agreement, Matthews said.
But as long as they were revising the documents anyway, Matthews said, system officials decided to see if they could get a lower interest rate.
That was a long shot because the state loan was low-interest to begin with, but it was worth a shot because interest rates had fallen so much in the last six years, he said.

The system advertised for bids Monday to convert the debt to $7.195 million of general obligation bonds, specifying that bids should retain the quarterly payment structure, and contain no prepayment penalty.

"We said, 'If you can come in and give us enough money to pay off the existing loan and (cover) the cost of issuance ... we will repay you over the remaining 14 years in equal quarterly payments,'" Matthews said. "They would have had to come in with 4.74, roughly, to take care of the cost of issuance."

Matthews said no disclosure documents were prepared because the issue would have been considered a private placement. Without the cost of preparing documents, "The worst that could happen is they lose the cost of the newspaper ad," he said.
What probably doomed the deal, Matthews said, is that it was not bank-qualified.
The sewer system plans a subsequent $17 million revenue bond issue and did not want to "blow its bank-qualified base" with this one, he said.
"That eliminated a lot of people. If it had been bank qualified I think some of the locals would have bid," Matthews said.
